The Center for Open Science and the Framework for Open and Reproducible Research Training are [collaborating for the SMART competition](https://www.cos.io/blog/cos-and-forrt-partner-to-increase-discoverability-and-usability-of-replication-evidence). As a result, FORRT will provide validated training data to competition participants. This report describes the data provided alongside it.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Terminology

The relation between an article reporting a replication study and the corresponding original study can be complex. The following terms allow for almost every combination of original and replication studies to be documented in the dataset.

+--------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Term   | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

| Entry  | One entry consists of a pair of studies, one of which self-identifies as a replication of the other, using different data than the original study. The replication study investigates at least one central claim from the original report. Each entry has been coded by two independent FReD Data Curators and validated by either a FReD Data Curator or a member of the FReD Core Team. Two entries may originate from the same study but not from the same sample. |
|        |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|        | One entry consists of at least one row but can consist of hundreds of rows: For example, some entries have multiple pairs of original and replication findings (e.g., for many different sub-groups) or do not have a 1:1 correspondence between original and replication study/reference but a different ratio. When assigning entries to FReD Data Curators, entries with overlapping studies are typically assigned to the same FReD Data Curator pair.            |
+--------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Study  | A study is an empirical investigation made in one of the reports. One entry usually consists of exactly two references/reports. Each of the references/reports can consist of multiple studies.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
+--------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Row    | One row in the database consists of one pair of original and replication effects that correspond to a claim made in the original study. In other words, one row is one pair of *findings*.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
+--------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Claim  | Each row must contain a claim that was made in the original report and that is tested again in the replication report. Multiple rows from one entry can have the same claim (e.g., a claim is tested using multiple statistical tests). Specific differences between identical claims are noted in a *description* variable.                                                                                                                                          |
+--------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

### Internal Process

Entries are drawn from the [FORRT Replication Database](https://forrt-replications.shinyapps.io/fred_explorer/), which consists of crowdsourced data that has been single-coded and partially validated, an unsystematic list of additional replications we have maintained, and a planned systematic literature search. A snapshot description of the FORRT Replication Database from October 2023 was published [here](https://doi.org/10.5334/jopd.101). In the starting phase of the data curation process, large-scale replication projects have been prioritized so that psychology replications make up the majority of the dataset. Over time, we expect greater disciplinary diversity in the reports.

Each entry is assigned to two FReD Data Curators, who independently complete all variables. They are collected by the FReD-team in a Google Spreadsheet for validation and run through a [cleaning-script](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forrtproject/FReD-data/refs/heads/main/clean_cos_fred.R). Most of the time, the values from one Data Curator are revised and chosen and the others are superseded. It is possible to choose a combination or all of the rows of an entry if different effects were coded by the FReD Data Curators.

### Computation of Standardized Effect Sizes

Based on the function that we use for effect size conversion, not all effects were converted to *r*. For exact computation details, see the [function in the FReD R package](https://forrt.org/FReD/reference/convert_effect_sizes.html). Please note that the choice of effect sizes conversions is particularly complex for test statistics and effect sizes that do not express an unconditional bivariate relationship (e.g., interaction effects or partial correlations) so that we leave the choice of whether and how to convert those to individual analysts. Please also note that some effect sizes are non-directional (e.g., R² or F-statistics), which is why we did not convert them despite functions being available. In these cases, the quantitative replication results will not show whether the pattern matches (e.g., two F test could be significant due to opposite interaction patterns).

+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Action                                                                                     | Effect Size Types                                                                                                      |
+============================================================================================+========================================================================================================================+
| Use as correlation                                                                         | r, Phi                                                                                                                 |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Convert to correlation                                                                     | Odds Ratio, Cohen's d, Hedges's g, test statistics (t test), Z values                                                  |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Convert but beware the lack of information about specific effect size pattern or direction | R², Eta squared, test statistics (F test), Cohen's f, Cohen's f², partial Eta squared                                  |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| No conversion                                                                              | test statistics (Chi-squared test, proportion test, binomial test), partial correlation, Cohen's dz, Cramer's V, Omega |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

```{r effectsize conversion, include = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(warning = FALSE, message = FALSE) 

# convert original effect sizes
ds$r_o <- convert_effect_sizes(es_values = ds$es_value_o, es_types = ds$es_type_o)  

# convert replication effect sizes
ds$r_r <- convert_effect_sizes(es_values = ds$es_value_r, es_types = ds$es_type_r)
```

### Success variable

There are many different indicators of replication success (many of which can be calculated with the [FReD package](https://forrt.org/FReD/articles/success_criteria.html)). However, for this project COS defines success as a significant result *in the same direction* as the original finding.

This is not trivial to derive from the data where effect sizes are not directional. Therefore, we provide a `replication_success` variable that is defined as follows:

-   `TRUE` when the replication is significant (based on the reported p-value, at alpha = .05) and the reported effect size is directional and in the same direction as the original. Note that this includes cases where effect sizes cannot be converted into a common metric, such as regression coefficients.

-   `FALSE` when the replication is not significant, or the reported effect size is directional and in the opposite direction as the original.

-   `NA` when the replication effect size is not directional (e.g, Eta squared, F-tests, R²) or when the original study was not significant (or did not report an effect size, so that the direction cannot be obtained programmatically).

<details>

<summary>Click here for a list of directional and non-directional effect size types</summary>

-   *Directional:* odds ratios, correlations (r and phi), Cohen's d / Hedges' g, t-test, Z, regression weights (b, beta), mean difference

-   *Non-directional:* η² (and partial), F-test, R²

</details>

```{r success, include = TRUE, echo = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.show = TRUE)

# directional effects
dir_types <- c("d", "r", "OR", "phi", "b (unstd)", "beta (std)", "beta", 
               "Mean difference", "percentage difference", "hedges' g",
               "median difference")

ds <- ds %>% 
  mutate(es_type_o = str_trim(es_type_o),
         es_type_r = str_trim(es_type_r))

ds <- ds %>% mutate(
  p_val_temp_r = coalesce(as.numeric(pval_value_r), FReD:::p_from_r(r_r, as.numeric(n_r))),
   p_val_temp_o = coalesce(as.numeric(pval_value_o), FReD:::p_from_r(r_o, as.numeric(n_o))),
  convertible = 
    (es_type_o %in% dir_types | str_detect(es_value_o, "^t|^Z|^z")) & 
       (es_type_r %in% dir_types | str_detect(es_value_r, "^t|^Z|^z")),
  replication_success = case_when(
    !convertible |  p_val_temp_o > .05 | 
      (p_val_temp_o == .05 & pval_type_o == "g (>)") | is.na(es_value_o) |
      is.na(es_value_r) | is.na(p_val_temp_r) | is.na(p_val_temp_o) ~ NA,
    (p_val_temp_r < .05 | (p_val_temp_r == .05 & pval_type_r == "l (<)")) & 
    sign(if_else(!is.na(r_r), r_r, as.numeric(es_value_r))) == 
    sign(if_else(!is.na(r_o), r_o, as.numeric(es_value_o))) ~ TRUE,
    .default = FALSE
  )) %>% 
  select(-convertible, p_val_temp_r, p_val_temp_o)
```

```{r scatterplot, echo = FALSE}
df_temp <- ds
df_temp$replication_success <- as.character(df_temp$replication_success)
df_temp$replication_success[is.na(df_temp$replication_success)] <- "uncertain"
df_temp$replication_success[df_temp$replication_success == "TRUE"] <- "yes"
df_temp$replication_success[df_temp$replication_success == "FALSE"] <- "no"

scatterplot <-
  ggplot(df_temp, aes(x = r_o, y = r_r, text = description)) +
    geom_point(aes(color = replication_success)) +
    scale_color_manual(
      name = "Replication Success",
      values = c("yes" = "#2ECC40", "no" = "#FF4136", "uncertain" = "grey50"),
      breaks = c("yes", "no", "uncertain"),
      labels = c("yes" = "Yes", "no" = "No", "uncertain" = "Uncertain")
    ) +
    geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0), linetype = 2) +
    geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, color = "Grey60") +
    scale_x_continuous(name = "Original Effect Size", limits = c(0, 1), breaks = c(0, .25, .5, .75, 1)) +
    scale_y_continuous(name = "Replication Effect Size", limits = c(-.5, 1), breaks = c(-.5, -.25, 0, .25, .5, .75, 1)) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(legend.position = "top")
    
    plotly::ggplotly(scatterplot, tooltip = "text") %>%
      plotly::config(displayModeBar = FALSE) %>%
      plotly::layout(xaxis = list(fixedrange = TRUE), yaxis = list(fixedrange = TRUE))
```

### Outcome variable (Ground truth)

::: callout-warning
**Please note that as of 18 September 2025, the outcome variable not yet fully double-coded and validated.**
:::

Given the complexity of deriving the success of a replication based on multiple statements, findings, methods, and theories, an alternative pathway to defining the success relies on the replication authors' judgment. From this perspective, they are seen as the experts of the original and replication studies and there is no need to apply a formal method to derive replication success solely from statistical parameters.

The outcome variable has been coded on a replication **study level** (as opposed to the claim level of the success variable) and can be *successful, failed, mixed, uninformative, or statistically successful but flawed*.

For cases where the outcome can be coded from the abstract, an LLM and a human coder independently determine the outcome. Other cases are coded by two human coders (e.g., multi-study articles). Outcomes for all cases are validated by a person.

***Outcomes***

We trust the replication authors whether they describe results as clear (successful or failed) or mixed. There are two special cases:

-   *uninformative* should is coded if the replication authors explicitly say so, e.g., because their sample was too small

-   *statistically successful but flawed* refers to replications where that is *the main message* (e.g., “we replicated x using the original methods, but show that they are not a valid test of the hypotheses”)

***Data source***

During determining the values, we looked at the most prominent quote that summarises the outcome (abstract \> conclusion \> discussion \> results).

***Level***

If there are multiple replication studies of the same target study in a paper, we tried to code what the authors say about each individual study (if they have different results).\

```{r outcome, echo = FALSE}

# leave only one entry per fred_id
ds_outcome <- ds[!duplicated(ds$fred_id), ]

# create table with outcomes for plotting
oc <- as.data.frame(table(ds_outcome$outcome, useNA = "always"))
names(oc) <- c("outcome", "freq")

oc$percent <- oc$freq / sum(oc$freq)

# plot
ocplot <- ggplot(oc, aes(x = factor(outcome, levels = c(
    NA, 
    "statistically successful but flawed",
    "uninformative",
    "failed",
    "mixed",
    "successful"
  )),
  y = freq,
  fill = factor(outcome, levels = c(
    "successful",
    "mixed",
    "failed",
    "uninformative",
    "statistically successful but flawed",
    NA
  ))
)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "successful" = "lightgreen",
    "mixed" = "orange",
    "failed" = "red",
    "uninformative" = "grey",
    "statistically successful but flawed" = "darkgrey",
    "NA" = "black"
  )) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Frequency",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . / sum(oc$freq) * 100, name = "Percent")
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "Outcome") +
  theme_minimal()

plotly::ggplotly(ocplot, tooltip = "freq") %>% 
      plotly::config(displayModeBar = FALSE) %>%
      plotly::layout(xaxis = list(fixedrange = TRUE), yaxis = list(fixedrange = TRUE))

```

### Codebook

The finalized dataset includes the variables that COS and FORRT agreed on as well as further variables that FORRT found necessary to understand the entered value. More detailed datasets are available upon request. A synthesis of the current version of the FORRT Replication Database with the new data's format is planned for fall 2025.

```{r codebook, echo = FALSE}

codebook <- openxlsx::read.xlsx("cos_codebook.xlsx")

DT::datatable(codebook, extensions = 'FixedColumns', options = list(pageLength = 300, dom = 't', rownames = FALSE, scroller = FALSE), rownames = FALSE)

```
